chunk_findings.detail: The new check tests for the substring `'id="D1"'` anywhere in the brief, not for a record whose actual `id` attribute is `D1`. Given a task whose files include `ledger/core/money.py` (`governs_d1` is true) but whose brief omits the D1 record and instead contains another record or text that merely mentions `related_id="D1"` (for example `<ddflow-record kind="decision" id="D2" related_id="D1">...`), the substring is present, so `('id="D1"' in brief) == governs_d1` is true and the check passes even though the governing D1 decision was not surfaced. This is the same class of false pass the fix was supposed to remove.
chunk_findings.title: demos/lifecycle_support.py:32

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate still does a raw substring search, not token matching. For a D1-governed file, `work(sc, client, tmp_path, wt_root, "P1.T1", {"ledger/core/money.py": "x=1"})` with a brief such as `<ddflow-record kind="decision" data-id="D1">` gives `('id="D1"' in brief)` as `True` because the substring appears inside `data-id="D1"`; `governs_d1` is also `True`, so the check passes even though no `id` attribute contains `D1`. That contradicts the comment's "match that token, not the bare substring" and leaves a false-positive bypass of the brief check for this input.
chunk_findings.title: demos/lifecycle_support.py:32

chunk_findings.detail: The `work` function in `demos/lifecycle_support.py` uses the local variable `files` inside the `governs_d1` check before `files` is defined in the execution flow. Looking at `demos/lifecycle_support.py`, `brief = client.tool("ddflow_brief", item=item)[0]` occurs at line 21, and the `files` parameter is only unpacked or iterated over later in the function (at `for rel, body in files.items():` on line 38), leading to an immediate `NameError: name 'files' is not defined` when `work()` is invoked with a `files` argument.

chunk_findings.detail: The new table assertion can pass vacuously. It slices `inspect.getsource(MC)` from the first occurrence of `RESOURCES: tuple` to the first occurrence of `RESOURCE_BY_URI`, but it never checks that the end marker is after the start marker or that the resulting slice is non-empty. For example, if `_core.py` contains `RESOURCE_BY_URI` in a module docstring, comment, or forward annotation before the actual `RESOURCES` tuple, then `start > end`, `table` becomes `""`, and `assert "fold(" not in table and "EventLog" not in table` passes even if the real resource table contains `fold(` or `EventLog`. It also no longer checks the `RESOURCE_BY_URI` mapping line itself or any code between that line and `class Server`, so a violation such as `RESOURCE_BY_URI = {r.uri: r for r in RESOURCES if not fold(r)}` would be missed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_roborev_findings.py::test_every_mcp_resource_is_served_through_the_cli

chunk_findings.detail: The added comment asserts that monkeypatching `ddflow.infra.log.install_kind` now reaches the same name that both `upgrade_remedy` and `skew_message` call, but the diff only inserts the call-time `from . import install_kind` inside `upgrade_remedy`. `skew_message` in the same module is not changed, so it still calls the `install_kind` object bound at import time. A caller or regression test that monkeypatches `ddflow.infra.log.install_kind` and then invokes `ddflow.infra.log.skew_message(...)` will still observe the pre-patch install kind, so the pre-split behavior remains broken for one of the two promised functions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_skew.py:41

chunk_findings.detail: The added `assert start < end` only rejects the case where the first `RESOURCE_BY_URI` occurs before the first `RESOURCES: tuple`; it still slices to the first occurrence of the marker. If `_core.py` has a docstring or comment before the real definitions that mentions both markers in order, e.g. `"""RESOURCES: tuple ... RESOURCE_BY_URI ..."""`, then both `start` and `end` are inside that docstring, `start < end` passes, and `table` is just the docstring fragment. The real `RESOURCES` tuple after the docstring can contain `fold(` or `EventLog`, but those characters are outside the slice, so the assertion passes and the test falsely proves the table is clean.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_roborev_findings.py::test_every_mcp_resource_is_served_through_the_cli

chunk_findings.detail: Replacing `index` with `rindex` still does not anchor the slice to the real module-level definitions; it only selects the last textual occurrence of each marker. If `_core.py` contains a trailing comment, docstring, or later function that mentions both marker strings in order, e.g. `# RESOURCES: tuple is indexed by RESOURCE_BY_URI`, then `start` and `end` land in that trailing text, `table` becomes only that fragment, and the `fold(` / `EventLog` assertion can pass even when the actual `RESOURCES` table contains `fold(` or `EventLog`. Conversely, if a later helper mentions `RESOURCE_BY_URI` and legitimately contains `fold(` or `EventLog`, `end` extends into that helper and the test fails even though the resource table is clean. The earlier vacuous-slice concern is therefore not fully answered by using `rindex`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_roborev_findings.py:317-318

chunk_findings.detail: The `rindex` change still does not ensure the slice is the real `RESOURCES` table. `rindex` finds the last textual occurrence anywhere in `inspect.getsource(MC)`, including post-definition comments or string literals. For example, if `_core.py` ends with a comment like `# Keep RESOURCES: tuple above in sync with RESOURCE_BY_URI.` after the real table, then `start` and `end` both point inside that comment, `start < end` passes, and `table` is `" above in sync with "`. The real table earlier could contain `fold(` and `EventLog` and the test would still pass, so the regression test can still be defeated by a trailing marker mention.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `EC.commit_at` can advance `wt.base` after `landed_before` has already been captured on the preceding line. When the primary has an uncommitted shard, `EC.commit_at` creates a new commit on the base branch before `W.merge` runs. If the merge then fails (for example, the existing conflict path where `c.txt` conflicts), `_landed_anyway` is called with the stale pre-event SHA while the base has already moved to the event commit. The branch has not landed—the modified test still asserts `main:c.txt` is unchanged—but the landing-check helper receives a baseline that no longer represents the state before the merge attempt, so it can misclassify the failure or report a false “landed anyway” note. The event commit should happen before `landed_before` is read, or `landed_before` should be refreshed after `EC.commit_at`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:188

chunk_findings.detail: `EC.commit_at` runs before `W.merge` and does not know whether the merge will succeed. In the refusal case with a primary event shard plus a `c.txt` conflict, `main` gets a new shard commit and only then `W.merge` returns `REFUSED`; the CLI reports failure but the primary branch has moved. The change acknowledges this by deleting the old `rev-parse HEAD` equality assertion in `tests/test_merge_primary_clean.py` and replacing it with a weaker `main:c.txt` content check, so a failed merge no longer guarantees the primary was left where it was.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:188

chunk_findings.detail: `EC.commit_at(log, cfg, "merge", f"merge {item}")` is called unconditionally during `merge` even when the merge will ultimately fail due to file conflicts (such as in `test_merge_primary_clean` where `c.txt` conflicts). This causes the primary's uncommitted event shards to be committed to `main` as part of a failed merge operation, altering the repository state and committing uncommitted work even though the merge itself was refused and rolled back.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:186

chunk_findings.detail: `glob_clashes` still keeps only `pairs[0]` per conflicting other item in both the live branch (`out.append(Clash(other_id, pairs[0], lease))`) and the offered branch (`out.append(Clash(other_id, pairs[0]))`). Given a live lease held by `sw-cedefaults` on `brief.py`, `lane_views.py`, and `reporting.py`, and a claim whose globs overlap all three, `conflicts()` returns three pairs but this function returns one `Clash` containing only the first pair. Since the `Clash` object carries no claim-glob list and no remaining pairs, `clash_report` cannot recover the dropped globs, so the refusal still names only one conflicting glob. Previous findings #1 and #5 still hold.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/admission.py:glob_clashes

chunk_findings.detail: The queue-behind messages now print `ahead.globs`, which is the whole set of globs the ahead lease asked for, not the subset of the refused item's own globs that are queued behind it. Given a refused item asking for only `brief.py`, while the ahead lease holds `brief.py`, `lane_views.py`, and `reporting.py`, the new text says `those files (brief.py, lane_views.py, reporting.py) are queued behind ...`, even though only `brief.py` is the refused item's blocked glob. This overstates the conflict and does not pair the refused glob with its actual queue place. Previous finding #2 still holds.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim_guard_queued.py:25, ddflow/api/lifecycle/reservations.py:201

chunk_findings.detail: `clash_report` returns `[oid for oid, _lz, _p in clashes]` without deduplicating item ids. Once one other lease overlaps more than one of the refused item’s globs — the multi-glob case this change is meant to surface — `_ids` contains that lease’s item id once per pair, e.g. `["B", "B"]` for two globs on the same other item. The docstring promises “every conflicting item id (a waiter must wait on each)”, so a caller that uses `_ids` to append wait dependencies will wait on `B` twice. The id list should be deduplicated while keeping all text clauses.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/common.py:clash_report

chunk_findings.detail: `clash_report` still has only the `held by {lz.holder} on {oid}` rendering and no queue-place branch. The bug this change fixes explicitly includes the `update --globs` path printing `those globs are queued behind sw-cedefaults` without naming a glob. For a queued clash passed through this function, the new text will assert `held by ...` even though the conflicting lease is only queued, and it still never states the queue place. The function needs a distinct “queued behind” branch for queued leases.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/common.py:clash_report

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that both glob strings (`src/a.py`, `src/b.py`) and both holder strings (`HOLDER`, `agent-holder2`) appear anywhere in `main`; it never checks which holder is paired with which glob. An implementation emitting `"src/a.py ... held by agent-holder2 ..."` and `"src/b.py ... held by HOLDER ..."` would still pass, even though the entire promise is to list every conflicting glob with its correct holder. The test must assert the paired clauses, not independent substrings.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_wait_claim_agree.py:test_claim_refusal_lists_every_conflicting_holder

chunk_findings.detail: The regression still does not exercise the `update --globs` queued path from the bug report. It only covers two live holders. A queued refusal that merely echoes the refused item’s own glob list and prints “queued behind sw-cedefaults” without naming the glob would still pass this test, so the stated bug can remain and the regression would stay green. The test should include an `update --globs` scenario with a queued lease and assert the conflicting glob plus queue place are named.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_wait_claim_agree.py:test_claim_refusal_lists_every_conflicting_holder

chunk_findings.detail: A mode-only change to a `.py` file is classified as trivial even though it is not a docs, format-only, or comment-only edit and can change runtime behavior. Given a commit that only does `chmod +x script.py` (100644 → 100755) on a file whose bytes already contain a shebang, `git diff HEAD -- script.py` is empty, then `_ast_unchanged` compares `git show base:script.py` with `git show HEAD:script.py`; those blobs are identical, so `diff_is_trivial` returns True. The behavior-changing executable-bit change then skips `rubber_duck`, `critic`, and `ci`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docsonly.py:_is_format_or_comment

chunk_findings.detail: The comment-only tier is limited to `*.py` files because `_ast_unchanged` hard-fails at `if not p.endswith(".py"): return False`. A task whose only diff is a comment fix in a non-docs, non-Python file such as `pyproject.toml` still gets `False` from `diff_is_trivial` and pays full cross-family review plus whole-suite `ci`, so the stated new comment-only change tier is not implemented for non-Python comments.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docsonly.py:_ast_unchanged

chunk_findings.detail: The logic-change regression only asserts that at least one of `rubber_duck`, `critic`, or `ci` remains in the pipeline (`or`). A behavior-preserving-tier bug that still leaves `rubber_duck`/`critic` but drops the whole-suite `ci` would satisfy `s.pipeline = ["rubber_duck", "unit_tests"]`, so the test passes even though the stated invariant is that logic changes must still pay full cross-family review **and** whole-suite `ci`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_trivial_tier.py:87 in `test_a_logic_change_does_not_accept_the_trivial_tier`

data.reason: 3 finding(s)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_find_body` treats any bare word `case` in a `$()` body as the start of a `case` statement because it calls `_case_end` for `_bare_word(text, n, k, "case")` without requiring `case` to be in command position. For input
`echo $(echo case)\ngit push origin main`,
the scanner sees the argument `case`, calls `_case_end`, never finds an `esac`, scans to the end of the whole input, and skips over the real newline after the outer `)`. `_logical_lines` therefore returns one logical line containing that newline as data instead of two command-position lines. `_split` then shlexes `echo $(echo case)\ngit push origin main` as one shlex invocation with the newline as whitespace, so `git push` is not treated as the start of a command and the forbidden command is missed. The word `case` here is an argument to `echo`, not a case statement.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body

chunk_findings.detail: The parametrized input `"echo ok >#x; git push origin main"` should not be refused. In a POSIX shell, `#` starts a comment when it begins a word. After the `>` redirection operator, the next word is `#x`, so `#x; git push origin main` is a comment to the end of the line; the shell does not execute `git push` at all (and the redirection is missing its target). Asserting `r is not None` for this case forces the guard to reject a command that is purely in a comment, which is a false positive and contradicts the test's own comment rationale. Use an input where the `git push` is actually executed, such as after `#` on a new line or with the `#` quoted.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_forbidden_commands.py:test_refused_comment_quote_spans_lines

chunk_findings.detail: `_case_end` only skips single quotes, `$'...'`, comments, and backslashes, so a bare `esac` inside a double quote or nested substitution ends the `case` early. `_find_body` then treats the next `)` as the end of the outer `$(...)` and the following `"` as an unclosed double quote. Given `$(case x in "$(echo esac)") git push origin main;; esac)`, bash runs `git push` when `x` matches `esac`, but the recorded body stops at `$(echo esac)` and the rest of the script is swallowed as quoted text, so the guard never sees `git push`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_case_end

chunk_findings.detail:
Comment detection only treats `#` as a comment when the previous character is in ` 	
;|&`. After a closing `)` or `}`, bash starts a comment and the quotes in it are not shell quotes. Given `(true)#'
git push origin main
'`, bash runs `git push`, but `_scan` opens a single quote at the comment's `'`, does not cut that newline, and hands shlex one quoted span, so `git push` is data rather than a command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_scan

chunk_findings.detail:
`_find_body` treats any bare word `case` in a `$()` body as the start of a `case` statement because it calls `_case_end` for `_bare_word(text, n, k, "case")` without requiring `case` to be in command position. For input
`echo $(echo case)\ngit push origin main`,
the scanner sees the argument `case`, calls `_case_end`, never finds an `esac`, scans to the end of the whole input, and skips over the real newline after the outer `)`. `_logical_lines` therefore returns one logical line containing that newline as data instead of two command-position lines. `_split` then shlexes `echo $(echo case)\ngit push origin main` as one shlex invocation with the newline as whitespace, so `git push` is not treated as the start of a command and the forbidden command is missed. The word `case` here is an argument to `echo`, not a case statement.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body

chunk_findings.detail: The parametrized input `"echo ok >#x; git push origin main"` should not be refused. In a POSIX shell, `#` starts a comment when it begins a word. After the `>` redirection operator, the next word is `#x`, so `#x; git push origin main` is a comment to the end of the line; the shell does not execute `git push` at all (and the redirection is missing its target). Asserting `r is not None` for this case forces the guard to reject a command that is purely in a comment, which is a false positive and contradicts the test's own comment rationale. Use an input where the `git push` is actually executed, such as after `#` on a new line or with the `#` quoted.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_forbidden_commands.py:test_refused_comment_quote_spans_lines

chunk_findings.detail: `_case_end` only skips single quotes, `$'...'`, comments, and backslashes, so a bare `esac` inside a double quote or nested substitution ends the `case` early. `_find_body` then treats the next `)` as the end of the outer `$(...)` and the following `"` as an unclosed double quote. Given `$(case x in "$(echo esac)") git push origin main;; esac)`, bash runs `git push` when `x` matches `esac`, but the recorded body stops at `$(echo esac)` and the rest of the script is swallowed as quoted text, so the guard never sees `git push`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_case_end

chunk_findings.detail:
Comment detection only treats `#` as a comment when the previous character is in ` 	
;|&`. After a closing `)` or `}`, bash starts a comment and the quotes in it are not shell quotes. Given `(true)#'
git push origin main
'`, bash runs `git push`, but `_scan` opens a single quote at the comment's `'`, does not cut that newline, and hands shlex one quoted span, so `git push` is data rather than a command.
